TRIPSPLIT  /  PRODUCT DESIGN2026  ·  CASE STUDY
PROJECT AT A GLANCE

An end-to-end mobile concept for planning trips with friends, using a consistent four-person Goa scenario.

01   ROLEProduct designer

UX flows, information architecture, visual system, and mobile screens

02   FOCUSThree everyday decisions

What’s next, what’s agreed, and what everyone owes

03   OUTPUT10 mobile screens

From creating a trip through planning, voting, and settlement

04   RESEARCH PLANInterviews with friends

Interview questions prepared; findings to be added after conversations

01 PROJECT OVERVIEW

One trip.
One shared picture.

TripSplit is a mobile product concept for friends planning travel together. It brings activities, group choices, and shared expenses into a single trip workspace, so each member can see the same up-to-date information.

THE DESIGN QUESTION

How might we reduce the effort of coordinating a trip without taking the spontaneity out of traveling together?

10Mobile interface screens
4Workspace destinations
3Core jobs: plan, decide, split
3–8Friends per group (target)
MY ROLE

UX and interface design—from defining the problem and mapping flows to wireframes, visual design, and final screens.

SCOPE

A complete visual design concept, including a design system and the principal trip-planning and expense-management journeys.

DELIVERABLES

Ten high-fidelity mobile screens, a scenario-based persona, information architecture, and documented design decisions.

02 THE PROBLEM

Four friends. Five days.
Too many loose ends.

For the design scenario, Ananya, Rohan, Neha, and Sameer are planning a Goa trip from 12–16 December 2026. They have bookings, ideas, and shared costs—but no single view that distinguishes a settled plan from an open question.

GOA12–16 Dec 2026
4Travelers
2 / 4Water-activity votes
₹12,400Group spending
01 / PLANNING

Is this activity confirmed?

Fort Aguada is fixed. Water sports in Baga is only proposed. Both appear in the trip schedule, but they shouldn't carry the same status.

02 / DECISIONS

Who still needs to respond?

Two members have voted for a water activity and two have not. Without that context, the group can't tell whether a choice is ready to finalize.

03 / EXPENSES

Has that payment cleared?

Rohan owes ₹1,900. Reporting a ₹1,000 transfer is not the same as Ananya confirming she received it.

DESIGN CHALLENGEMake the difference between planned, agreed, and paid immediately clear to everyone on the trip.

The Goa trip, travelers, and amounts are a consistent example used to develop and examine the interface.

03 RESEARCH APPROACH

Understand the last trip.
Not the ideal one.

I planned to speak with friends who have organized or joined group trips, because they could describe real planning situations. The interview guide focuses on what happened during a recent trip, which tools were involved, and where coordination became difficult.

INTERVIEW PLAN

Small, varied conversations

Speak with around 3–5 people who have organized or joined trips with friends. Include both the person making arrangements and someone who mainly follows along.

Format20–30 minute semi-structured conversations
FocusReal examples, workarounds, disagreements, and repayment tracking
CareVoluntary participation, anonymized notes, no private payment details
THE MESSAGE I PREPARED FOR FRIENDS
“I'm exploring a better way to organize trips with friends. Could I ask you about the last group trip you went on—how everyone decided what to do, and how you handled shared expenses? I'm interested in what actually happened, even the messy parts.”

Ask for permission to take notes. Avoid pitching the app until after the discussion, so answers aren't shaped by the proposed solution.

01

Walk me through the last trip you organized with friends.

02

How did the group know which plans were final?

03

Tell me about a shared expense that needed settling.

Research stage: Friend interviews are the next step. This case study documents the interview approach and question guide, while findings will be added after those conversations are completed.

04 USER PERSONA

The friend who ends up
keeping everyone aligned.

Rohan is a scenario-based persona built from the Goa trip example. His situation keeps the interface focused on one traveler's goals, frustrations, and decision-making needs.

SCENARIO-BASED PERSONA
Rohan, 24
Young working professional
Often becomes the person who keeps the trip on track
NEEDS ONE CLEAR NEXT STEP
HIS SITUATION

Starting a plan is easy.
Keeping everyone informed isn't.

Rohan is comfortable suggesting activities, but he doesn't want to chase confirmations or repeatedly ask where the group is meeting. He also wants to know his balance without opening a separate expense sheet.

GOALS

See the next confirmed activity, know when his vote matters, and understand what he owes.

FRICTIONS

Decisions buried in chat, ambiguous activity status, and unsettled payments that look completed.

WORKAROUNDS TO VALIDATE

Checking screenshots, searching old messages, and asking the organizer to confirm details.

PRODUCT OPPORTUNITIES

One shared itinerary, visible group participation, clear costs, and separate payment-confirmation states.

Moment that matters

The water-sports vote is still open at 2/4 responses. Rohan can cast his vote and check his ₹1,900 outstanding balance without guessing which updates are final.

05 ASSUMPTIONS TO TEST

What could change
after the interviews?

The interface is built around three working assumptions. These are questions for research, not findings. Each has a clear design implication if the conversations point in another direction.

01

Plans get lost or misunderstood.

To examine: where people look for the current itinerary and how they know a decision is final.

Could change: how prominent the Plan tab and confirmation badges should be.

02

Group choices need visible participation.

To examine: how often friends actually vote versus settle decisions in conversation.

Could change: whether polls belong in persistent navigation or as an activity-level tool.

03

Expense confirmation builds trust.

To examine: how groups check a transfer was received and what records they keep.

Could change: how much detail the settlement flow needs.

06 INFORMATION ARCHITECTURE

A place for every question.
No maze to get there.

The trip workspace stays organized around four recurring needs. Tasks that require attention—creating a trip, adding an expense, or reporting a payment—open focused screens and return users to the workspace.

OverviewWhat's coming up, and what needs attention?
PlanWhere are we going, and is it confirmed?
PollsWhat are we still deciding?
ExpensesWhat has been spent, and who owes whom?
01 / START A TRIP

My Trips → Create Trip → Invite Friends → New Trip

02 / MAKE A DECISION

Trip Overview → Polls → Vote → Organizer confirmation

03 / SETTLE A COST

Expenses → Add Expense / Settle Up → Recipient confirmation

Why separate the forms? Workspace tabs support frequent switching. Focused screens keep short, consequential actions easier to scan.
07 DESIGN DECISIONS & ITERATION

Less uncertainty.
More useful information.

The interface changed as the different jobs of planning, deciding, and settling became clearer. Three decisions shaped the final screens.

01 / NAVIGATION

Four places to return to.

Overview, Plan, Polls and Expenses stay visible in the workspace. Create Trip, Add Expense, and Settle Up use focused layouts.

Tradeoff: fewer shortcuts inside forms, less competition for attention.
02 / ACTIVITY STATUS

Proposed is not confirmed.

The group's water-sports idea appears as pending while Fort Aguada is confirmed. A decision needs an explicit final step.

Tradeoff: one more action, fewer misleading itinerary entries.
03 / PAYMENTS

Reported is not received.

A ₹1,000 payment report stays pending against Rohan's ₹1,900 debt. Only the recipient's confirmation changes the balance to ₹900.

Tradeoff: more careful bookkeeping, more reliable balances.
A REAL BEFORE–AFTER

The Trip Overview, from structure to experience

The grayscale wireframe established information priority. The final screen adds destination context, better visual grouping, and clearer status treatment.

EARLY WIREFRAMEHierarchy first
FINAL INTERFACETravel context + clear states

08 VISUAL DESIGN SYSTEM

Made for the trip.
Built around clarity.

The visual direction takes its energy from coastal travel: turquoise water, bright destination photography, and warm accents. Utility screens use quieter surfaces and strong contrast, because financial information should feel calm and dependable.

Color and meaning

Teal identifies key actions; mint supports completed or confirmed information; warm yellow marks decisions still in progress.

Sea teal#078F83 · Actions
Deep ink#123C3C · Headlines
Soft mint#DFF8F1 · Support
Coral#FF7258 · Emphasis
Warm sand#FFF1CC · Pending
Paper#F5F9F8 · Background

Type, components, and rhythm

Your trip starts
with a plan.

Inter typography, clear size contrast, 18–20px mobile insets, generous tap targets, and consistent card spacing. Icons support labels rather than replacing them.

Primary actionDestination card✓ Confirmed◷ Pending vote
Accessibility intention

Status labels use words as well as colors. Financial amounts are prominent and aligned for comparison; icon-only actions are limited to familiar controls.

10 WIREFRAME TO FINAL UI

The structure stayed.
The experience became warmer, clearer, and more desirable.

The low-fidelity wireframe established hierarchy, core actions, and navigation logic. The final interface kept that foundation, then added stronger visual focus, travel imagery, richer status cues, and more inviting interaction surfaces.

Early wireframeLOW FIDELITY

The early version focused on content order and task clarity: what the next activity is, where trip information lives, and how users move into polls, itinerary, and expenses.

Final interfaceHIGH FIDELITY

The final UI uses imagery, layered cards, stronger color contrast, and more polished data presentation to make the same flow feel more intuitive, lively, and confidence-building.

01 · VISUAL PRIORITYThe hero area now highlights the most relevant trip context first instead of treating all information with the same weight.
02 · EMOTIONAL TONETravel photography and softer surfaces make the product feel more aspirational while still preserving utility.
03 · DECISION SUPPORTStatuses, balances, and next steps are surfaced more clearly so users can act quickly without interpreting the interface.
11 KEY SCREEN HIGHLIGHTS

A closer look at the decisions
inside the final UI.

These annotated callouts make the design intent easier to understand in a portfolio setting. They explain what each screen is doing, not just what it looks like.

Trip OverviewENTRY POINT
1
Shared trip context comes first

The hero card surfaces destination, dates, and the most immediate trip snapshot so users understand the state of the trip immediately.

2
Status chips reduce ambiguity

Pending and confirmed states help the group distinguish what is final from what still needs attention.

3
Quick access to core tasks

Itinerary, polls, and expenses are visible as clear destinations, reducing the need to hunt through the interface.

Group PollsDECISION MAKING
1
Active and closed polls are separated

The segmented control makes it easy to focus on what still needs input versus what has already been decided.

2
Each option includes enough context

Voting cards pair a label with visual cues and vote progress so the choice feels more tangible and easier to compare.

3
Results connect back to planning

The screen reinforces that poll outcomes are not isolated — they are meant to shape the itinerary.

ExpensesFINANCIAL CLARITY
1
Top summary answers the main question fast

The total spend, your share, and current amount owed appear before the expense history so the user gets clarity immediately.

2
History is readable at a glance

Each row combines category, payer, and amount in a clean format that reduces cognitive load during review.

3
Settlement is always within reach

The path to settling balances is introduced within the same screen, supporting a smoother transition from review to action.

Settle UpTRUST & CONFIRMATION
1
The interface recommends a useful next payment

Instead of exposing a complex ledger first, the screen starts with the simplest meaningful action the user can take.

2
Confirmation protects shared trust

The design makes it explicit that a reported payment is not treated as settled until the recipient confirms it.

3
Transparent history prevents confusion

Settlement records and status cues help everyone understand what has been paid, what is pending, and why a balance still remains.

12 FINAL APPLICATION UI

Ten screens. One coherent journey.

The complete mobile interface, grouped by the tasks travelers return to most often. Each screen supports a specific point in the trip journey.

13 REFLECTION

The hard part wasn't
putting everything on a screen.

It was deciding which details could be simplified—and which needed to stay explicit. A trip can be visually exciting, but uncertainty about plans and money should never be hidden under visual polish.

A useful group workspace should answer three questions quickly: What's next? Have we agreed? What do I owe?
WHAT IMPROVED

More recognizable trip context, clearer confirmed-versus-pending states, and a cleaner hierarchy around spending and balances.

WHAT TO VALIDATE

Whether friends actually need dedicated polls, how they track changing plans, and what payment-confirmation evidence feels sufficient.

WHAT I WOULD DO NEXT

Complete the planned interviews, revise assumptions where necessary, and test comprehension of the most consequential screens.

TripSplit is a concept project built around a consistent trip scenario. The persona helps frame the design, while interview findings and product outcomes remain future validation work.

A INTERVIEW GUIDE / APPENDIX

Questions for the first conversations.

Fourteen open-ended questions about recent group trips, organized so a conversation can follow real experiences instead of hypothetical feature preferences.

01 / Recent trip & tools

  1. Tell me about the most recent trip you planned with friends. Who was involved, and what was your role?
  2. Walk me through planning that trip, from the first idea to the final plan. Which tools did you use?
  3. Where did you keep dates, addresses, booking details, and activity ideas? What was easiest or hardest to find later?

02 / Planning & changes

  1. Think of a time the group changed its plans. What triggered the change, and how did everyone find out?
  2. How did your group decide which activities were confirmed and which were still suggestions?
  3. When you were actually traveling, how did you check what was next or who needed to be where?

03 / Decisions & participation

  1. Tell me about the last time people wanted different activities, restaurants, or dates. What happened?
  2. How did you know who had shared their preference and who had not replied?
  3. What happened when someone changed their mind or a decision needed to be made quickly?

04 / Money & reflection

  1. Walk me through a shared expense from that trip. Who paid, and where did you record it?
  2. When expenses were uneven, how did you decide who should contribute how much?
  3. How did you check that someone had actually paid you back, or that you had settled your share?
  4. Which moment in the overall planning process felt most frustrating or uncertain, and why?
  5. If you could change one part of your group-trip planning process, what would it be?

Useful follow-up prompts

  • “Can you tell me exactly what happened next?”
  • “What made you choose that approach?”
  • “How did you know the group had agreed?”
  • “Could you show an example, with private details hidden?”

Use follow-ups to understand specific moments. Ask about the app concept only after the behavioral questions.
